cover.topic: Pottery, farm life, language and kelp forests

sections.title: Enrolling in a pottery course
sections.context: You will hear a man phoning a pottery studio in Fremantle to enrol in a course.

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: Good morning, Harbourside Clay Studio, Marcia speaking.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Hi there. I saw your poster in the Fremantle library, and I'd like to enrol in a pottery course for the winter term. Is it too late?

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: Not at all, we've still got a few places left. Have you done any pottery before?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Only a one-off workshop years ago, so I'm basically a beginner.

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: That's fine. We run three beginner courses. There's hand building, which is all coils and slabs, there's a glazing and decorating course, and there's wheel throwing.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Well, wheel throwing is the one I've always wanted to try. You know, the whole spinning the clay thing.

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: It's our most popular course, but it's messy and a bit frustrating at first, so be warned.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: I'll risk it. How many people are in each group?

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: We keep it to ten, so everyone gets a turn at the wheels and I can come round and help each person individually.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: That sounds ideal. Can I put my name down now?

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: Of course. Let me open the enrolment form. What's your surname?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: It's Harcourt.

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: Could you spell that for me?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Sure. That's H-A-R-C-O-U-R-T.

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: Lovely, thank you. And a contact number?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: My mobile's 0412 555 038.

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: 0412 555 038. Got it. Now, the wheel throwing course runs on Tuesday evenings, from six until eight.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Oh, that's a shame. I work late on Tuesdays. Is there any other night?

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: Let me check. Actually, yes. We have a second group on Wednesday evenings, same time, and there are still four places in it.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Wednesday would be perfect.

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: Great, I'll book you into that one. The course is eight weeks long. The Tuesday group starts on 15 July, but the Wednesday group begins a week later, because the studio is closed for the school holidays.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: So that's 22 July for me?

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: That's right, 22 July. Now, the fee. It's 340 dollars for the eight weeks, and that includes all your clay and the firing of your first six pieces.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Hmm, that's a little more than I expected. Is there any kind of discount?

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: Well, if you pay before the end of this month, we take 25 dollars off. So you'd pay 315 dollars.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: That's much better. Can I pay online?

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: Yes, I'll email you a payment link as soon as we finish this call.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Great. And where exactly is the studio? I only know it's somewhere near the harbour.

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: We're at 62 Whaler Street, in the old fishing district.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Sorry, was that 26 Whaler Street?

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: No, it's 62. Six, two. It's the green building with the big sliding door, just opposite the bakery.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Got it. And what's the postcode, so I can put it in my phone?

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: It's 6160, the same as the rest of central Fremantle.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Perfect. Is there anything I need to bring on the first night?

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: Just an apron, because you'll get covered in clay, and it helps if you keep your fingernails short. We provide all the tools and the wheels, so there's no need to buy anything yourself.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Okay, I'll dig out an old apron. What about parking?

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: There are a few bays outside the studio, but they're limited to two hours, and your class is longer than that. Most of our students use the Dock Street car park. It's free after five o'clock, and it's only a two-minute walk.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: That sounds easy enough. Do you ever hold an exhibition of the students' work?

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: We do. At the end of every term we put on a small show in the front room, and family and friends are welcome. Some of our students even sell a few pieces.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Ha, I don't think mine will be ready for that. But I'm looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: You'll be surprised how quickly you improve. Is there anything else you'd like to ask?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: No, I think that's everything. Thank you very much for your help, Marcia.

transcript.speaker: Marcia
transcript.text: You're welcome, Tom. I'll send that email now, and we'll see you in July.

sections.title: Open day at a Tasmanian farm
sections.context: You will hear a guide welcoming visitors to an open day at a dairy and sheep farm in the Huon Valley.

transcript.speaker: Gwen
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Fernbrook Farm open day here in the Huon Valley. My name's Gwen, and I look after our visitors, so if you have any questions today, just look for the people wearing the green caps. Before you head off to explore, I'd like to go through a few practical things.

transcript.speaker: Gwen
transcript.text: First, parking. Some of you have already left your cars in the river paddock, which is where we used to send people. However, we've had a lot of rain this week and the ground down there is very soft, so for the rest of the morning please use the top paddock, next to the main gate. It's a little further to walk, but there's a free trailer ride every ten minutes, pulled by one of our tractors, which the children usually enjoy more than the farm itself.

transcript.speaker: Gwen
transcript.text: Now, entry. Adult tickets are 12 dollars, and children between five and fifteen pay 6 dollars. Children under five are free. A few people have asked about discounts for library members or for people on our mailing list, but I'm afraid those only apply to our winter events, not today. Your ticket is a wristband, so keep it on, because you can leave and come back as often as you like.

transcript.speaker: Gwen
transcript.text: A word about dogs. I know many of you would love to bring yours along, but because we have lambs and calves around, we can't allow dogs on the farm at all, even on a lead. We've built a small fenced pen next to the car park, with water and shade, so you can leave your dog there, but please check on it every so often.

transcript.speaker: Gwen
transcript.text: Next, the cheese. Many of you have come specifically for our cheese-making demonstration, and I'm happy to say that you don't need to book in advance, which is what people often ask. But please note that it only runs once, at eleven o'clock, and the cheese room holds just thirty people, so I'd suggest arriving early. Children are very welcome, by the way, although they have to stay with an adult.

transcript.speaker: Gwen
transcript.text: Another thing people ask about is the shearing demonstration, which you'll see on the programme is at two o'clock. Some of you have wondered why it isn't in the morning, when it's cooler. People often assume it's because the shearer is busy elsewhere, but no, he's here all day. The real reason is that the sheep need to be completely dry. The paddock was soaked by rain overnight, and shearing wet wool is difficult for the shearer and bad for the sheep. So we wait until the afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Gwen
transcript.text: Now let me tell you what's on offer at each stop, so you can plan your day. Just inside the gate, on your left, is the dairy shed. Milking takes place at half past one, and you can watch our cows being milked by machine. Children can also see how the milk travels into the cooling tank. I should warn you that you can't taste the milk there, because it's raw, but there's fresh milk for sale in the shop.

transcript.speaker: Gwen
transcript.text: Further along the lane you'll find the orchard. The apples are in season right now, and we have three varieties ready. Pick up a basket at the entrance, choose your own fruit straight from the trees, and we'll weigh it on the way out. Please try not to climb the trees, because the branches are fragile. Bear in mind that the plant stall, where you can buy seedlings and herbs, is up by the car park, not in the orchard.

transcript.speaker: Gwen
transcript.text: The third stop is the cheese room itself. It's open all day, not only during the demonstration, and you can taste the cheeses, yoghurt and honey that are produced right here on the farm. People tend to buy a lot, so do leave room in the car.

transcript.speaker: Gwen
transcript.text: After that, follow the track up the hill to the sheep paddock. Our ewes had their lambs about three weeks ago, so if you walk in quietly, you'll be able to see the newborn lambs close up. I'm afraid we can't let you feed them, because they're still too young. We're not running guided walks this year, by the way, so you're free to wander at your own pace, but please keep to the marked tracks.

transcript.speaker: Gwen
transcript.text: And finally, there's the old barn, which was built in the eighteen nineties. The local historical society has put together a display of photographs showing the farm over more than a century, along with the tools that the early settlers used. You may recognise some of the faces, because several families in the valley still have relatives in the pictures.

transcript.speaker: Gwen
transcript.text: The café is next to the barn, and it's serving lunch from half past twelve. If you would like to have lunch at the long tables outside, please remember to put your rubbish in the bins, because the wind can carry it into the paddocks. That's everything from me. Enjoy your day, and thank you for supporting a family farm.

sections.title: A project on Māori words in New Zealand English
sections.context: You will hear two linguistics students, Aroha and Ben, discussing their project with their tutor, Doctor Hughes.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: Come in, you two. Right, let's go through your project proposal. Remind me, it's about Māori words in New Zealand English?

transcript.speaker: Aroha
transcript.text: That's right. We want to find out how often people our age use words like kai, whānau and mahi in everyday conversation, and whether the habits differ between regions.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: It's a good topic. How did you come up with it, Aroha? Was it the sociolinguistics lecture last term?

transcript.speaker: Aroha
transcript.text: Well, that gave me the vocabulary to describe it, but no, the real start was my job. I work in a café on weekends, and customers drop those words into their orders all the time without thinking about it. I started noticing it and I couldn't stop.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: And I just thought it would be easier than my other idea, which was accents in sport commentary.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: Honesty is always welcome, Ben. Now, the questionnaire. I've read the draft. It has thirty questions, which is far too many for people to answer in a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: Aroha
transcript.text: We thought that more data would be better.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: More data is only better if people actually finish. I'd cut it down to about twenty. Also, you haven't asked where participants grew up, and for a regional comparison that's essential.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: You're right, we forgot that completely. We can add it at the top.

transcript.speaker: Aroha
transcript.text: What if we asked people to answer out loud instead of writing? I think they'd be more natural.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: It's an interesting idea, but you'd have to transcribe every answer, and that would take weeks. Stick with written responses.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: What about offering a small prize? Like a gift voucher for one lucky participant?

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: Possibly, but you'd need extra approval for that, and you don't have a budget. I'd leave it out.

transcript.speaker: Aroha
transcript.text: Okay, so shorter, plus the question about where people grew up.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: Exactly. Now, the second part of your plan is recording real conversations.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Yes, and I'm a bit worried about that part. People tend to go stiff and formal as soon as they know a recorder is switched on, so we won't hear how they really talk.

transcript.speaker: Aroha
transcript.text: But we could do it in a café, where everybody's relaxed.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: That's the observer's paradox, and every researcher faces it. Recording in a relaxed place helps, and so does starting with a few minutes of small talk that you don't use. I wouldn't worry too much about the transcription either, since you'll only be transcribing short extracts.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: And the permission forms?

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: They're a bit tedious, but they're quick once you have the template.

transcript.speaker: Aroha
transcript.text: Speaking of the café, my manager has said we can record there on Sunday mornings, as long as we put a notice on the door.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: That's very helpful, and it's worth mentioning in your methods section. Make sure that the notice also explains what the recording is for, and who will hear it.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Should we also give people a chance to say no afterwards, once they've heard themselves?

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: Yes, you should. Participants need to be able to withdraw their conversations for a couple of weeks afterwards. Put that on the permission form, in plain language.

transcript.speaker: Aroha
transcript.text: We'll add a line about it, and a contact email, in case anyone changes their mind.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: Good. Also think about how many recordings you need. Ten short conversations is a sensible target, rather than aiming for something huge.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Ten is much more realistic than the twenty we first wrote down.

transcript.speaker: Aroha
transcript.text: Now, about the literature review. Should we focus on research from the last twenty years? Most of the interesting studies are recent.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: I'd be careful about that, because you'd miss the foundation. Begin with a short history of the contact between Māori and English, no more than a page, and then move to the recent work.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Could we compare with Canada? There's research on how Canadian English borrowed words from Indigenous languages.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: It's tempting, but it would take you away from your question. Keep to New Zealand.

transcript.speaker: Aroha
transcript.text: Fine. Could we go through the timeline now? I've drawn up a plan.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: Please. Let's start with the ethics application. You'll fill in the form, of course, but it can't be submitted until the head of department has signed it, and she's often away, so don't leave it until the last minute.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Understood. Then we planned a pilot survey about three weeks after that.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: Good. I'd suggest you test it on the other group working on the phonetics project, so you get honest feedback quickly. Don't just try it on your friends.

transcript.speaker: Aroha
transcript.text: Okay. We've allowed two weeks for collecting data.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: I think that's optimistic. Recruiting people always takes longer than students expect, so I'd allow at least a month.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: That will make things tight, but we'll manage. For the analysis, we were going to use the statistics software in the computer lab.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: You don't need to. You can reach it through the university website from home, so you can work whenever you like.

transcript.speaker: Aroha
transcript.text: That's a relief. Finally, there's the presentation, and we thought we might just improvise.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: Please don't. Practise it at least twice in front of your classmates, because you'll find the awkward moments that way. A handout is optional, but a good one always helps.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Right. Thanks, Doctor Hughes. This was really useful.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hughes
transcript.text: You're welcome. Send me the revised questionnaire by Friday, and I'll take another look.

sections.title: Kelp forests
sections.context: You will hear a marine science lecturer giving a talk on kelp forests.

transcript.speaker: Professor Reid
transcript.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to talk about kelp forests, which are among the most productive ecosystems on the planet, even though most people never see them. I'll start with the basic biology, then look at what lives in them, and finally at why they are disappearing and what we might do about it.

transcript.speaker: Professor Reid
transcript.text: First, a common misunderstanding. Kelp is not a plant. It's a type of brown algae, and it belongs to a group that is only distantly related to the plants on land. Kelp has no true roots, stems or flowers, and it takes in nutrients directly from the surrounding water through its surface. That is why it is found mostly in cool, nutrient-rich water. In general, kelp grows best where the water temperature stays below 20 degrees Celsius. Above that, it becomes stressed and its growth slows.

transcript.speaker: Professor Reid
transcript.text: Within those limits, kelp can grow astonishingly fast. Giant kelp, which is the species we see around southern Australia and the Pacific coast of Canada, can grow up to 60 centimetres in a single day. A strand can reach thirty or even forty metres in length within one growing season, which makes it one of the fastest growing organisms on Earth.

transcript.speaker: Professor Reid
transcript.text: Let me describe the structure, because it explains a lot. At the bottom, kelp is anchored to rocks by a root-like structure called a holdfast. Many people assume this absorbs nutrients like a root does, but it only holds the kelp in place, and a great many small animals actually live inside it. Above the holdfast is a long stalk, and along the stalk are the blades. Each blade has a small gas-filled bladder at its base, and these bladders keep the fronds floating upwards, so that the blades stay near the surface where the sunlight is strongest. That arrangement allows the kelp to photosynthesise efficiently even when the water below is dark.

transcript.speaker: Professor Reid
transcript.text: Now, what lives there? A kelp forest is a three-dimensional habitat, a bit like a rainforest under the sea. The canopy shelters fish from predators and from strong waves, and the water beneath it is calmer than the open ocean. Young fish use the forest as a nursery, and so do juvenile rock lobster, which are an important commercial species in both Tasmania and New Zealand. Larger animals, such as seals and many seabirds, hunt in and around the forest, and the whole system supports a huge fishing industry.

transcript.speaker: Professor Reid
transcript.text: But kelp forests are fragile, and one of the key reasons is a small animal, the sea urchin. Urchins feed on kelp, and normally the amounts they eat are not a problem. However, when urchin numbers explode, they can strip the seabed of almost all its kelp. What is left is called an urchin barren, a rocky area covered in urchins and almost nothing else. Once a barren forms, it can stay that way for decades, because the urchins can survive on very little food and they stop young kelp from re-establishing.

transcript.speaker: Professor Reid
transcript.text: What controls urchin numbers? In many places, it's predators. On the Pacific coast of North America, for example, sea otters eat urchins, and where otters were hunted almost to extinction, the kelp forests collapsed. When otters were reintroduced to parts of British Columbia, the kelp slowly returned. In Australia, rock lobster and large fish play a similar role, which is why overfishing can indirectly damage kelp.

transcript.speaker: Professor Reid
transcript.text: The other big threat is warming water. Along the east coast of Tasmania, the East Australian Current has been pushing warm water further south for several decades. The giant kelp forests there were once huge, and the loss has been dramatic. Surveys show that about 95 percent of the giant kelp has disappeared since the nineteen sixties. Warm water has two effects. It stresses the kelp directly, and it also allows urchins from further north to spread south, so the problems feed each other.

transcript.speaker: Professor Reid
transcript.text: So, what can be done? There are several approaches, and I'll mention three. First, divers have been removing urchins by hand from small areas, which allows kelp to recover quickly. That works, but it's slow, and it costs a great deal. Second, scientists are collecting kelp that has survived in warmer water, and breeding it in the laboratory, hoping to produce strains that tolerate heat. And third, researchers are testing ways of restoring forests by growing young kelp in tanks and then attaching it to ropes, which are laid out on the seabed. The ropes protect the young plants from grazing until they are large enough to survive, and early trials in Tasmania look promising.

transcript.speaker: Professor Reid
transcript.text: Let me finish with a point about the value of these forests. Apart from their role in the food chain, kelp absorbs carbon dioxide, and it also softens waves, which protects shorelines during storms. Some companies are even harvesting kelp for food and fertiliser, though there is a debate about whether harvesting wild kelp is sustainable. For next week, please read the two articles on the course page, and think about whether restoring a kelp forest is realistic or whether we should instead put our effort into reducing the causes of warming. We'll discuss it then.
